items.headline: Scientists propose new test for hidden features of merged black holes
items.title: Do black holes have hidden hair? Scientists find a new way to check
items.scifi_hook: Merging black holes ring like cosmic bells, revealing clues about unseen hair.
items.eli5: When two black holes smash, the new one vibrates and the fading waves may show hidden stuff.
items.why: It could confirm or challenge fundamental physics about black holes.
items.text: When two black holes crash together and merge, the newly formed black hole rings like a bell, sending out gravitational waves with specific frequencies that fade over time. This brief, fading pattern of waves is called ringdown, and it may hold secrets about what is hiding around black holes.

items.headline: Isar Aerospace's Spectrum becomes Europe’s first fully commercial orbital rocket
items.title: German company becomes first in Europe to launch fully commercial orbital rocket
items.scifi_hook: A German startup lofted a private rocket from the Arctic to orbit in seven minutes.
items.eli5: A two‑stage rocket built by a German company launched from Norway and reached space on its first try.
items.why: It adds new competition to Europe’s launch market and may lower costs.
items.rationale: more launch options could boost demand
items.text: Isar Aerospace, founded in 2018 by three students at a German university, successfully launched a privately-developed rocket into low-Earth orbit Saturday from a Norwegian spaceport inside the Arctic Circle. The two-stage rocket, named Spectrum, became the first fully commercial launch vehicle in Europe to reach orbit. With Saturday's success, Isar is the clear leader among a pack of several European launch startups vying to inject some competition into Europe's stagnant launch market. Isar's 92-foot-tall (28-meter) Spectrum rocket lifted off at 4:12 pm EST (20:12 UTC) Saturday from Andøya Spaceport in northern Norway, where it was 10:12 pm local time as the final bluish hues of daylight faded from the late summer sky. Seven minutes later, the rocket was in orbit. Read full article Comments

items.headline: Chinese tech powers Egypt’s 1.1 GW Obelisk solar farm
items.title: Chinese technology powers Africa's largest solar farm in Egypt
items.scifi_hook: A 1.1‑GW Egyptian solar farm runs on Chinese robots and battery storage.
items.eli5: China’s tech powers Egypt’s huge solar plant and its big batteries to keep lights on.
items.why: Large clean‑energy project boosts grid reliability and cuts fossil fuel use.
items.text: Egypt is expanding its solar power capacity with help from Chinese technology. The Obelisk solar project in southern Egypt generates about 1.1 gigawatts of electricity and features large-scale battery storage to support the national grid. The $600 million project also uses automated systems and solar-powered robots to improve efficiency and maintain the panels. Meanwhile, rural communities are adopting smaller solar projects to reduce their reliance on unreliable power grids.
